lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Words can heal hearts. Today, we climb the cloud stairs at the very top of Heart Hill. The steps are soft and white, and they bounce a little under our feet. Birimo bounces the most. At the top, a huge door opens, and we walk into the Hall of the Round Table. In the middle stands a giant round table with a world map painted on it. Above the table floats a small, friendly globe with a big smile. He spins and says, Welcome, friends! I'm Orbit, the chair of this table. Every voice counts! Six children are sitting around the table with their teachers. Amina is from Africa, Priya is from Asia, Nadia is from Europe, Sam is from North America, Mateo is from South America, and Liam is from Oceania. One chair is empty. It's for Antarctica. Orbit laughs. No children live there, but the penguins send their hello! Haru says, Children from every continent sit at this table. Say it with me. Children from every continent sit at this table. Excellent! Orbit points to a golden sign on the wall. Let's read the sign. "Welcome to the Hall of the Round Table. At this table, children from every continent meet to talk about our big, beautiful world. We share what we know, we listen to different ideas, and we look for answers together. In four weeks, this hall will hold the Children's World Conference. Every child at the table will have a chance to speak, and you will make new friends from all over the world. Around the table stand six lanterns. Right now, they are all dark. Each time you learn a new way of working together, something wonderful will happen. Remember, there are no small voices here. Every voice counts!" When is the Children's World Conference? In four weeks. How many lanterns are there? Six, and right now they are all dark. Kiko touches one lantern gently. It feels cool and quiet, as if it is waiting for us. Now, phonics. Many environment words are built from parts. Environment is environ plus ment, so don't forget the n before the m. Sustainable is sustain plus able, so it can keep going. Renewable is re plus new plus able, so it can be made new again. Next time, we'll have lunch at the hall and learn about food.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Children from every continent sit at this table. Today, it's lunchtime at the Hall of the Round Table. There is a long buffet with rice, bread, noodles, soup, salad and fruit from every continent. Birimo grabs the biggest plate he can find. He takes three rolls, two bowls of noodles, a mountain of rice and five pancakes. The mountain is taller than his head! He eats and eats, and then he leans back and holds his tummy. I can't eat another bite! Sam looks at all the leftovers and smiles kindly. He says, In my town, we learned something surprising. About one third of food is wasted. Say it with me. About one third of food is wasted. Well done! Birimo's face turns pink. Oops. Sorry, food! Orbit spins over to us and shows us a fact card. Let's read it. "Food Facts from the Round Table. Around the world, about one third of all the food we grow is never eaten. Some food goes bad on farms, some is thrown away at shops, and some is left on plates at home and at school. When food is wasted, the water, land and hard work that went into it are wasted, too. But here is the good news. People everywhere are finding ways to help. Many schools now let children take smaller servings and come back for more. Some families plan their meals and turn leftovers into new dishes, like fried rice or soup. Every bite we eat instead of throwing away makes a difference." How much food is wasted around the world? About one third. What can families do with leftovers? They can make new dishes, like fried rice or soup. Birimo takes a small plate this time and wraps up his extra rolls to share later. Now, phonics. More environment words are built from parts. Pollution comes from pollute. Drop the e and add ion. Recycle is re, which means again, plus cycle, which means circle. Conservation comes from conserve. Drop the e and add ation. Next time, Amina will tell us about clean water.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, About one third of food is wasted. Today, Amina from Africa shares a story with the whole table. She holds up a photo of her town. It is sunny and dry, with red earth and tall, shady trees. Amina says, When my mother was a girl, she walked a long way every morning to get water. She carried a heavy bucket home on her head. In some places, many girls and boys still do that today, so they have less time for school and play. Then Amina smiles. But last year, my town built a new well with a pump. Now the water is close to our homes. Orbit spins slowly and says, Around the world, millions of people don't have clean water nearby. Say it with me. Millions of people don't have clean water nearby. Very good! Amina passes around a letter she wrote for the table. Let's read Amina's letter. "Dear friends at the Round Table, I want to tell you about our new well. Before, the closest clean water was far away, near the next village. Girls and boys spent hours walking there and back. Last year, grown-ups from our town worked together with builders to dig a deep well. Now there is a strong pump right next to the market. You push the handle up and down, and clean, cool water comes out. My little brother says it is the best thing in town. Now girls and boys have more time for school, homework and football. Water is precious, so we use it carefully. From your friend, Amina." Where is the new pump? Right next to the market. What do girls and boys have more time for now? School, homework and football. Ms. Emma says, These are big problems, and you don't have to fix the whole world. Small actions count. If world news ever makes you feel worried, talk to a grown-up you trust, like a family member or a teacher. Now, phonics. Ecosystem is eco, which means home or nature, plus system. Deforestation is de, which means take away, plus forest plus ation. Global comes from globe. Drop the e and add al. Next time, Priya will tell us about a very special bus.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Millions of people don't have clean water nearby. Today, it's Priya's turn. Priya is from Asia, and her town is surrounded by green hills and rice fields. In the villages around her town, there aren't many schools or libraries. So every Saturday, a big, bright library bus drives from village to village. It is painted with elephants, stars and flowers, and it is full of books. Children run to meet it when they hear its happy horn. Orbit says that around the world, millions of children can't go to school. Some live too far away, and some have to help at home. Riko thinks for a moment and says, Every child should be able to go to school. Say it with me. Every child should be able to go to school. Wonderful! Priya shows us her blog post on a big screen. Let's read it. "Hi! This is the story of our library bus. Every Saturday morning, the bus leaves my town at eight o'clock. Our teachers and volunteers drive it along the hill roads to five villages. At each stop, they open the side doors, and shelves full of picture books, comics and science books appear. Children can borrow two books for one week. Some children are learning to read for the first time, so volunteers read stories aloud under a big tree. Last month, a girl told me she wants to be a doctor. Then she borrowed a book about the human body. Books open doors. I hope every child can have a chance to learn." How many books can children borrow? Two books for one week. What does the girl want to be? A doctor. Birimo jumps up and says, I'm playing the library bus! Beep beep! Books for everyone! Now, phonics. The blue pins show places where people are working to bring clean water closer to homes, like Amina's new well. The green pins show food waste. About one third of food is wasted, and this challenge affects many countries, including ours. The yellow pins show places where children are getting new chances to learn, like Priya's library bus. Each challenge is big, but each pin also has a card with good news. People are building wells, sharing food and driving books to villages. Thank you for listening. We hope you can help, too. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, From the farmer's point of view, every carrot is precious. Today, we look at food from a shop's point of view. Sam from North America tells us about his aunt. She runs a small grocery shop on a busy street, with baskets of apples, bananas and tomatoes out front. Every morning, she opens the doors at seven, and her neighbors stop by for fresh bread and fruit. Birimo asks, Why would a shop throw away good food? Sam explains that many customers pick only the shiniest, roundest apples. The ones with little spots stay on the shelf. Also, every package has a date label, and some people won't buy anything when the date is close. Riko nods and says, Shops throw away food because customers want perfect fruit. Say it with me. Shops throw away food because customers want perfect fruit. Nice job! But Sam's aunt had an idea. Let's read the notice in her shop window. "Hello, shoppers! Meet our new Wonky Veggie Boxes! Inside each box, you'll find carrots with two legs, bumpy potatoes, tiny apples and tomatoes in funny shapes. They look a little different, but they taste just as delicious. Each box costs less than regular vegetables, so you save money, too. And please remember, a best-before date tells you when food is at its best. Food is often still good after that date, so look, smell and ask a grown-up. Every box you buy helps farmers and keeps good food from being thrown away. Ask us about this week's box. Thank you for shopping with us!" What's inside a Wonky Veggie Box? Carrots with two legs, bumpy potatoes, tiny apples and funny-shaped tomatoes. What does a best-before date tell you? When food is at its best. Sam says the boxes sell out every Friday, and his aunt throws away much less food now! Now, phonics. Here are even bigger numbers. One billion has nine zeros. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Shops throw away food because customers want perfect fruit. Today, Liam from Oceania holds up a plastic water bottle. He says, Plastic is amazing in many ways. It's light, it's cheap, and it keeps food fresh. Then he shows us a photo of a beach near his home, with bottle caps and plastic bags in the sand. Ms. Emma teaches us a new linking word. When you connect a good point and a bad point, you can use however. Haru tries it. Plastic is useful. However, it can harm the sea. Say it with me. Plastic is useful. However, it can harm the sea. Perfect! Birimo gasps. Oh no! The sea is not a trash can! Liam nods. That's right, and the good news is that many people are helping. Liam's class decided to do something about it. Let's read his beach clean-up report. "Our Beach Clean-Up Report. Last Saturday, our class and our teachers held a beach clean-up. Everyone wore gloves, and the grown-ups picked up anything sharp. In two hours, we filled twelve big bags. We found bottle caps, straws, food wrappers and one very old flip-flop. Plastic is useful, because it keeps our sandwiches fresh. However, when plastic ends up in the sea, turtles and seabirds can mistake it for food. After the clean-up, we made a promise. We will bring reusable bottles to school and use lunch boxes instead of plastic bags. The beach looked beautiful, and a little crab came out to say thank you!" How many bags did the class fill? Twelve big bags. What did the class promise to bring to school? Reusable bottles. Birimo walks sideways and says, I'm playing the crab! Thank you, friends! Now, phonics. Let's say parts of a whole. One of two equal parts is half. One of three equal parts is one third. Two of three equal parts is two thirds. Thirds has an s, because there are two of them. Remember, about one third of food is wasted. Next time, we'll ask everyone at the hall some questions.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Plastic is useful. However, it can harm the sea. Today, Orbit asks us to do a survey. We ask the children and teachers at the hall the same three questions about recycling, water and food. Riko and Kiko hold clipboards, Haru counts the answers, and Birimo makes a very tall tally chart. In the end, we ask forty people. Nadia and Mateo even help us count the last answers, and everyone is very kind and patient. Haru looks at the results and shouts, Everyone recycles! But Ms. Emma smiles. Careful! Not everyone answered yes. Haru laughs. Oops! You're right. When we aren't completely sure, we can say it seems that. Riko tries it. It seems that more people are recycling. Say it with me. It seems that more people are recycling. Great! We can also say, This might mean that something is true. Let's read our survey results. "Round Table Survey Results. We asked forty children and teachers at the hall three questions. First, do you recycle more now than two years ago? Thirty people said yes. It seems that more people are recycling. Second, do you turn off the water while you brush your teeth? Twenty people said yes. That is half of the group. This might mean that many of us can still save more water. Third, do you always take only the food you can finish? Ten people said yes. That is a quarter. This might mean that many of us are still learning. We did not ask everyone in the world, so these results are only about our group." How many people said they recycle more? Thirty people. Why can't we say everyone? Because we only asked our group, and not everyone said yes. Now, phonics. A quarter means one of four equal parts. Fifty percent is the same as half. Seventy percent means seventy out of one hundred. Don't add an s to percent. About seventy percent of the Earth's surface is water. Next time, we'll put many points of view together in one big presentation.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, It seems that more people are recycling. Today, we give a big presentation to the whole Round Table. Amina, Priya, Nadia, Sam, Mateo and Liam sit with their teachers, ready to listen. Each of us holds a poster. Haru has the farmer, Riko has the shop, Birimo has the family, and Kiko has the sea. Ms. Emma teaches us two more linking words. Moreover adds another strong point. Therefore shows the result. Haru asks, Is moreover the same as and? Ms. Emma says, It's similar, but moreover sounds great in a presentation, and it adds a stronger point. Kiko practices the ending. Sharing food helps people. Moreover, it saves money. Therefore, we should share extra food. Say it with me. Moreover, it saves money. Therefore, we should share extra food. Brilliant! Now, let's read our presentation. "Today, we'd like to look at food from many points of view. From the farmer's point of view, every carrot is precious, even the funny-shaped ones. From the shop's point of view, it's hard to sell food that doesn't look perfect. However, wonky veggie boxes are helping. From a family's point of view, leftovers can become tasty new meals. From the sea's point of view, less plastic packaging means a cleaner home for turtles. When we share extra food with neighbors, fewer good things go to waste. Moreover, it saves money. Therefore, we should share extra food. Let's work together. Thank you for listening!" How many points of view did we talk about? Four: the farmer, the shop, the family and the sea. What does moreover do? It adds another strong point. The six children clap, and Orbit spins and spins. Every voice counts! Then the second lantern flickers and starts to glow with soft rainbow light. The Lantern of Many Views lit up! Two lanterns are shining now. Now, phonics. Let's review. One billion has nine zeros. One third means one of three equal parts. Renewable is re plus new plus able. Next time, Orbit will teach us about debates, where two teams take turns sharing different opinions.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Moreover, it saves money. Therefore, we should share extra food. Two lanterns are shining beside the round table now, and the Lantern of Many Views shines the warmest. This morning, Orbit spins slowly above the table and says, Every voice counts! Today, we'll learn how to have a debate. A debate（ディベート） is a special kind of talk. Haru looks a little worried. Is it a fight? Orbit laughs. Not at all! In a debate, two teams share different opinions. Say it with me. In a debate, two teams share different opinions. Great! One team says yes to a topic, and the other team says no. Both teams listen carefully and give reasons. Birimo puts on a pair of glasses with no glass in them. I'm playing a very serious judge! Hmm, hmm. Everybody giggles. Then a sign appears over the table. Let's read Orbit's debate rules. "Welcome to the Round Table Debate! Here are our six rules. Rule one: There are two teams. One team agrees with the topic, and the other team does not. Rule two: Take turns. Only one person speaks at a time, and everyone else listens. Rule three: Watch the timer. Each speaker has one minute, so speak clearly and don't rush. Rule four: Use reasons and facts. Don't just say, I'm right! Explain why. Rule five: Disagree with ideas, not people. You can say, I see your point, but... Never laugh at anyone. Rule six: When the debate is over, thank the other team. Remember, a debate is not about winning. It is about thinking more deeply, together. Every voice counts!" How long can each speaker talk? One minute. What should you do when the debate is over? Thank the other team. Amina raises her hand. In my class, we had a debate about longer lunch breaks. It was really fun, because I heard ideas I had never thought of. Mateo nods. And we all shook hands at the end. Now, phonics. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We believe that schools should have gardens. Today, the yes team needs reasons. Now put them in order. Start with, Our first point is. Haru stands up. Our first point is that gardens teach us about food. Say it with me. Our first point is that gardens teach us about food. Great! But a reason needs evidence, too. Evidence means facts or examples that show your reason is true. Mateo says, My uncle is a farmer. He says children who grow carrots usually want to eat them! Suddenly, Birimo wants a carrot, and everyone laughs. Let's read the yes team's reasons. "Our first point is that gardens teach us about food. In a garden, students plant seeds, water them and wait. They see how a tiny seed becomes a carrot or a tomato. For example, at Mateo's school in South America, children grow beans, and then they cook them for lunch. Many of them try new vegetables for the first time. Our second point is that gardens are good for our bodies and minds. Students dig, carry water and pull weeds, so they move a lot. Working outside in the fresh air can also help people feel calm. Let me give an example. When Riko feels nervous before a test, watering plants helps her relax. Therefore, we believe that schools should have gardens." What do the children at Mateo's school grow? Beans. What helps Riko relax? Watering plants. Orbit nods. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We disagree because gardens take a lot of time. Today is the big day: our first mini debate! All six children and their teachers sit around the round table to watch. Orbit floats in the middle with a little clock on his front. I am the timer today! Each speaker has one minute. Birimo bows to the audience. I'm playing a famous debate star! Orbit chuckles and spins once. Let's begin! Riko goes first and gives the claim. Beep! The minute is up. Orbit says, Thank you. Now, the other team, please. Say it with me. Thank you. Now, the other team, please. Perfect! A good chair always thanks the speaker and gives the next team a turn. Let's read the debate script. "Orbit: Welcome to our mini debate! The topic is, Schools should have gardens. Yes team, please begin. Riko: We believe that schools should have gardens. Our first point is that gardens teach us about food. Orbit: Thank you. Now, the other team, please. Kiko: We disagree because gardens take a lot of time, especially during the summer holidays. Haru: That's a fair point. However, families and teachers can take turns, and we can plant vegetables that grow before summer. Birimo: The other team said families could help. But not every family has free time. Orbit: Thank you, both teams. Every voice counts! Now, let's thank each other." Who gave the yes team's claim? Riko. What did Haru say about the summer? Families and teachers can take turns, and they can plant vegetables that grow before summer. Then all four friends stand up and shake hands. Orbit asks for a show of hands, just for fun. Amina, Sam and Liam vote yes. Priya, Nadia and Mateo vote no. It's a tie! Everyone laughs. Orbit says, Both sides had good points, and both teams were kind. That is the real win! Suddenly, the third lantern by the table begins to shine. The Lantern of Debate lit up! Now three lanterns shine together. Now, phonics. Let's review. We beLIEVE that: stress believe. We disaGREE because: stress agree. Half means one of two equal parts, and we write it as one over two. Pollution comes from pollute: drop the e and add ion. Next time, we'll put our heads together and look for solutions.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Thank you. Now, the other team, please. The mini debate was fun, but today Orbit has a new challenge. We've talked about problems. Now, let's look for solutions! A solution is an idea that helps fix a problem. Orbit spins over the part of the map that says food waste. Remember, about one third of food is wasted. What can we do about it? Sam raises his hand first. In my town, there is a sharing fridge at the community center. People put extra food inside, and anyone who needs it can take some. Haru's eyes go wide. Anyone? For free? Sam nods. Yes. A bakery brings bread at the end of the day, and families bring vegetables from their gardens. Riko writes on the solution board. One solution is to share extra food. Say it with me. One solution is to share extra food. Fantastic! Kiko adds another idea. At school, we could have a sharing shelf. If you don't want your apple, you put it on the shelf, and someone else can enjoy it. Birimo raises both hands. I'm playing a hungry squirrel! I'll take all the nuts! Ms. Emma laughs. Then the shelf wouldn't be fair, Birimo. Let's read the notice on Sam's sharing fridge. "Welcome to the Sharing Fridge! This fridge belongs to everyone in our neighborhood. Please share extra food that is fresh and clean, such as fruit, vegetables, bread and sealed packages. Please write today's date on a sticker before you put food inside. However, please don't bring raw meat or fish, because they go bad quickly. Volunteers check the fridge every morning and every evening. Therefore, the food stays safe and the fridge stays clean. Take what you need, and leave some for others. For example, last week a bakery shared twenty loaves of bread, and every loaf found a home. Thank you for helping us waste less food!" Why shouldn't people bring raw meat or fish? Because they go bad quickly. How many loaves of bread did the bakery share? Twenty. Now, phonics. Linking words guide the listener. Say the first part strongly and take a short pause after the comma. HOWever, pause, shows a different idea. THEREfore, pause, shows a result. For exAMple, pause, gives an example. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, One solution is to share extra food. Today, Nadia from Europe stands up with a photo of her town at night. In my town, we have a special evening once a month called Dark Sky Hour. For one hour, families turn off the lights they don't need. Shops turn off their big signs. Then everyone looks up at the stars. Wait, really? says Birimo. I'm playing a sleepy light bulb! Good night! He closes his eyes and pretends to snore. Nadia laughs. Saving energy is important, because making electricity can use a lot of fuel. When one family turns off one light, it saves a little energy. But imagine a whole town doing it. Orbit spins slowly. Let's imagine it together. If everyone turned off the lights, we would save energy. Say it with me. If everyone turned off the lights, we would save energy. Excellent! Notice the words turned and would. We use them to imagine something that isn't happening yet. Let's read Nadia's poster. "Dark Sky Hour in Our Town. On the first Saturday of every month, from eight to nine in the evening, we turn off the lights we don't need. Why? Making electricity can use a lot of fuel. Moreover, bright lights at night can confuse birds and insects. As a result of Dark Sky Hour, our town uses a little less energy every month. On the other hand, some people worry about safety in the dark. Therefore, the lights on busy roads and at train stations stay on. Families stay together at home or in the park, and many children see the Milky Way for the first time. Imagine this: if everyone in the world turned off one light for one hour, we would save a lot of energy together." When is Dark Sky Hour? On the first Saturday of every month, from eight to nine in the evening. Which lights stay on? The lights on busy roads and at train stations. Riko thinks for a moment and says, If everyone unplugged their chargers, we would save energy, too. Orbit spins happily. Every voice counts! Now, phonics. MoreOver adds a stronger point. As a reSULT shows what happens next. On the OTHer hand shows the other side. Pause after each comma. Next time, we'll look at small actions that children can do every day.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let's combine our ideas. Today, the friends turn their ideas into an action plan. Let's read the action plan. "Our Action Plan: The Sharing Fridge Project. Our goal: to waste less food in our neighborhood. Step one: Next week, we will ask the grown-ups at the community center if we can use an old fridge. Ms. Emma will help us write a polite letter. Step two: After that, we will make posters and practice Kiko's song. However, we will only put up posters where the community center says it's okay. Step three: At the end of the month, we will open the sharing fridge with our families and teachers. Grown-ups will check the fridge every day. We hope that fifty percent of the extra bread from the bakery will go into the fridge instead of the trash. Therefore, everyone can help, step by step." Who will help write the letter? Ms. Emma. Who will check the fridge every day? Grown-ups. Amina raises her hand. What happens if nobody uses the fridge? Haru thinks. Good question. Then we'll sing Kiko's song louder! Everyone laughs, and Riko adds, And we'll ask people why, and change our plan. Amina smiles. That's a smart answer. Orbit spins so fast that he sparkles. Every voice counts! lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Our action plan has three steps. Our sharing fridge plan is ready, and for the conference we will share a bigger idea for every school. Now the Children's World Conference is only one week away! This morning, Orbit floats above the round table and spins slowly. He says, Every voice counts! But every voice also needs a little time. So here is the rule for the conference. Each team will present for two minutes. Say it with me. Each team will present for two minutes. Great! Two minutes isn't very long, so we need to practice. Haru looks worried. Two minutes? I could talk about the sharing shelf for two hours! Birimo laughs and says, I'm playing a stopwatch! Tick, tock, tick, tock! Ms. Emma gives everyone a pile of small cue cards. Let's read Orbit's tips for the conference. "Getting Ready for the Children's World Conference. Each team will present for two minutes, so plan carefully. First, choose your most important idea. Don't try to say everything. Second, write only key words on your cue cards, not whole sentences. Then you can look up and smile at the audience. Third, decide who will speak first, second and last. Everyone on the team should have a part. Fourth, practice with a stopwatch. If you go over two minutes, cut something out. Finally, remember that it's OK to feel nervous. Take a deep breath, speak slowly, and look at a friendly face. The other children want to hear your ideas, and they will be on your side. Every voice counts!" What should you write on your cue cards? Only key words. What can you do if you feel nervous? Take a deep breath, speak slowly and look at a friendly face. In our first rehearsal, we talk for three minutes and twenty seconds. Oops! In our second rehearsal, Haru cuts his long story about the lunch tray, and we finish in one minute and fifty seconds. Perfect! Now, phonics. These words help us be careful when we are not one hundred percent sure. Seem means looks like. The audience seems friendly. Might means maybe. We might finish early. Probably means about eighty percent sure. We will probably feel nervous, and that's OK. Next time, the conference begins, and Kiko will give the opening speech.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Each team will present for two minutes. Today is the big day! The Children's World Conference begins. The Hall of the Round Table is full. Delegates from every continent sit around the table with their teachers, and families sit in rows behind them. Orbit floats in the middle with a tiny bell. Antarctica's chair is still empty, but there is a little card on it: Hello from the penguins! Orbit rings the bell and asks Kiko to open the conference. Kiko's hands are shaking a little. Riko whispers, You can do it. Kiko takes a deep breath, looks at a friendly face, and says, Welcome, everyone. Today, we'll talk about food waste. Say it with me. Welcome, everyone. Today, we'll talk about food waste. Wonderful! Let's read Kiko's opening speech. "Welcome, everyone. Today, we'll talk about food waste. I'm Kiko, and I'm here with my friends Haru, Riko and Birimo. Thank you for coming from every corner of the world. At lunch on our first day, we learned that about one third of food is wasted. That surprised us. Then we listened to farmers, shop owners and families, and we found out that the problem has many sides. We also learned that children can help. Today, each team will share an idea. Some ideas may seem small, but small ideas can grow. Please listen carefully, ask questions, and be kind. Perhaps by the end of today, we will find something we can all agree on. Let's begin!" What did the friends learn on their first day? About one third of food is wasted. What does Kiko ask the delegates to do? Listen carefully, ask questions and be kind. When Kiko finishes, the applause is so loud that Orbit spins three times. Birimo shouts, I'm playing the audience! Bravo! Bravo! Kiko's face is pink, but she is smiling from ear to ear. Now, phonics. Here are more careful words. Appear means seem, or look like. The audience appears happy. May means maybe. We may run out of time. Perhaps also means maybe. Perhaps we will all agree. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Welcome, everyone. Today, we'll talk about food waste. Kiko's opening speech went really well. Now it's our team's turn to present. Orbit starts his two-minute timer and spins once. Haru and Riko walk to the front of the round table with their cue cards. This will help reduce food waste. Say it with me. We propose that every school has a sharing shelf. This will help reduce food waste. Excellent! We propose that is a polite and strong way to suggest a plan at a meeting. Let's read our proposal. "A Sharing Shelf in Every School. We propose that every school has a sharing shelf. This will help reduce food waste. At lunch, students usually have some fruit or snacks left over. If you can't finish your food, such as a whole apple, a banana or a closed snack, you can put it on the shelf. Anyone who is still hungry can take it. Open food and food that needs a fridge cannot go on the shelf. Our posters will remind students to take only what they can eat, and our song will make sharing fun. A sharing shelf is cheap and easy to make. It will likely save a lot of food. It could possibly bring friends closer, too. Thank you for listening." Why is a shelf a good idea? Because it's cheap and easy to make. Which food cannot go on the shelf? Open food and food that needs a fridge. We finish in one minute and fifty-five seconds. Orbit spins happily and says, Every voice counts! Then hands go up all around the table. Now, phonics. Likely means it will probably happen. It will likely save food. Possibly means maybe, but we are less sure. It could possibly bring friends closer. Usually means most of the time, but not always. Students usually have some food left over. We, the children of the Round Table, come from many places, and we have many different ideas. We listened to each other, asked questions, and changed our plans when we heard good points. We all agree that no food should go to waste. Therefore, we promise to take only what we can eat, to share extra food kindly, and to tell our families and friends what we learned. We will probably not fix everything at once, and that's OK. Small actions, done together, can make a big difference. We will keep listening, because every voice counts. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We all agree that no food should go to waste. The first part of the conference is over, and five lanterns are shining around the round table. Today, Orbit gives us a new challenge: reading. He says, Before you give your opinion, read more than one side. Nadia has brought two short articles from her town's newspaper. Her town is thinking about turning off some street lights at night. Riko reads them and says, Article A and article B have different opinions. Say it with me. Article A and article B have different opinions. Great! Let's read the two articles. "Article A: Let the Night Be Dark. Our town has hundreds of street lights, and many of them shine all night on empty roads. Our main point is simple: we should turn some of them off after midnight. This would save energy and money. In addition, we could see the stars again. Night animals such as owls, moths and bats need darkness to find food and their way home. Article B: Keep Our Streets Bright. Some people walk home late from work, and bright streets help them feel safe. Lights also make it easier to see steps, bikes and cars. Older people may find dark streets difficult. It might seem like a small change, but everyone should feel comfortable outside at night. We believe that street lights are important for everyone. Both writers care about our town. Which article do you agree with?" What are the reasons in article A? To save energy and money, to see the stars, and to help night animals. Why does article B want to keep the lights on? People feel safe, and it's easier to see. Haru says, Article A is right! Kiko says, Wait, article B makes a good point, too. Ms. Emma smiles. That's exactly why we read both sides. Now, phonics. Let's review. Sustainable is sustain plus able: it can keep going. Ten million has seven zeros. Our main point is: say MAIN strongly. In addition adds another point, so pause after the comma. Seem means look like. Next time, we'll write an opinion essay that mentions both sides.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Article A and article B have different opinions. Today, Orbit asks each of us to write a short opinion essay about the street lights. He says a good essay is like a fair judge. It shows both sides, and then it gives your opinion with reasons. Riko starts her essay like this: Some people think street lights should stay on all night. However, I believe we can turn some off. Say it with me. Some people think street lights should stay on all night. However, I believe we can turn some off. Excellent! First, you show the other side. Then you say what you believe. Let's read Riko's essay. "Street Lights at Night. Some people think street lights should stay on all night. However, I believe we can turn some off. On the one hand, lights help people feel safe when they walk home, and they make it easier to see. This is an important point, and we should listen to it. On the other hand, many lights shine on empty parks and fields where nobody walks at night. These lights use a lot of energy, and they make it hard for owls and bats to find food. Therefore, I believe we should turn off the lights in empty places after midnight and keep the lights on busy streets. Perhaps we could also use sensor lights that turn on when someone walks by. In this way, people can stay safe, and night animals can enjoy the dark. We can take care of both people and nature." Which lights does Riko want to keep on? The lights on busy streets. What idea does Riko add near the end? Sensor lights that turn on when someone walks by. Kiko writes the opposite opinion, and her essay is fair and kind, too. Haru asks, Wait, really? We can have different opinions and still both be fair? Ms. Emma nods. Yes, of course! Now, phonics. Let's review. Conservation is conserve, drop the e, plus ation. Two thirds has an s, because there are two. We strongly believe: say STRONG strongly. On the other hand shows the other side. Perhaps means maybe. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Some people think street lights should stay on all night. However, I believe we can turn some off. Today, Orbit has a special idea. He says, Let's send a message from the Round Table to the whole world! All the children sit together. Priya suggests starting with Dear world. Sam wants to write about food, Amina wants to write about water, and Liam wants to write about the sea. Mateo says, Don't forget the farmers! Nadia adds, And the stars! Birimo wants a line about pancakes, but everyone laughs and says, Maybe next time. Then Kiko writes the first line: Dear world, we children want a cleaner and kinder planet. Say it with me. Dear world, we children want a cleaner and kinder planet. Lovely! Let's read our message. "Dear world, we children want a cleaner and kinder planet. About eight billion people live on Earth, and we all share one home. We came to the Round Table from every continent. We learned that big problems have many sides, and that listening is the first step. Let me explain why we are hopeful. People everywhere are already helping. Towns are building new wells, buses are bringing books to villages, and classes are cleaning beaches with their teachers. We will do our part, too. We will take only what we can eat, turn off lights we don't need, and share kindly. Please work with us. If everyone helps a little, our planet will likely become a better home for all of us. With love, the children of the Round Table." About how many people live on Earth? About eight billion. What will the children do? Take only what they can eat, turn off lights they don't need, and share kindly. Orbit rolls up the message and places it in the center of the round table. As a result, the whole table seems to hum softly. Now, phonics. Let's review. Global is globe, drop the e, plus al. Eight billion has nine zeros after the eight, and no s on billion. Let me explain why: say WHY strongly. As a result shows a result, so pause after the comma. Likely means it will probably happen. Next time, we'll say goodbye to our new friends around the hall.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Dear world, we children want a cleaner and kinder planet. Tomorrow is the closing ceremony, so today we take a goodbye walk around the Hall of the Round Table. We stop at our world map of challenges, which still has all our pins and cards. We remember Sam's lunch talk about food waste, Amina's new well, and Priya's library bus. We visit Mateo, whose uncle grows funny-shaped carrots, and Liam, who cleaned his beach with his class. We laugh about our garden debate, when Kiko and Birimo said gardens take a lot of time. Then we thank each of the six children. Haru says, You taught us to see things from many sides. Riko adds, We believe that every point of view matters. Say it with me. We believe that every point of view matters. Wonderful! Let's read our thank-you card. "Dear Amina, Priya, Nadia, Sam, Mateo and Liam, thank you for sharing your stories with us. Amina, your well showed us that clean water changes lives. Priya, your library bus showed us that books can travel. Nadia, you taught us to think about lights and stars. Sam, you helped us understand shops. Mateo, you made us love funny-shaped carrots. Liam, you showed us how to care for the sea. Before we came here, we usually thought there was only one right answer. Now we believe that every point of view matters. We will never forget you, and we will keep your stories in our hearts. Your friends, Haru, Riko, Kiko and Birimo." What did Priya's library bus show the friends? That books can travel. What did the friends usually think before they came? That there was only one right answer. The six children give us big smiles and warm hugs, and Orbit spins slowly, humming a happy tune. Now, phonics. Let's review. Endangered is en plus danger plus ed: it means in danger. A quarter is one out of four. The other team said: say OTHer strongly. In conclusion starts the end of your talk, so pause after the comma. Usually means most of the time. Next time, it's the grand closing ceremony of the Children's World Conference!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We believe that every point of view matters. Today is the closing ceremony of the Children's World Conference! The hall is full of families, teachers and children. Orbit floats above the round table, and five lanterns are shining around it. Only the sixth one is still dark. Orbit asks each team to share one hope for the future. Amina hopes every town will have clean water nearby. Priya hopes every child can go to school. Sam hopes no food will go to waste. Then Orbit asks everyone to stand, hold hands, and say it together. Together, we can make the world a better place. Say it with me. Together, we can make the world a better place. Fantastic! Let's read Orbit's closing words. "Dear children of the Round Table, four weeks ago, you came here with different languages, different homes and different ideas. You learned about the world's challenges. You looked at problems from many points of view. You debated kindly, found solutions, made a plan, and reached an agreement. Finally, you wrote a message to the whole world. Let me give an example of your kindness: whenever you had different opinions, you thanked each other. Some problems will possibly take many years to solve, but you have already started. Go home, share what you learned, and keep listening to each other. Together, we can make the world a better place. Every voice counts!" What did the children do when they had different opinions? They thanked each other. What should the children do when they go home? Share what they learned and keep listening. Suddenly, the sixth lantern begins to glow. The Lantern of Hope lit up! All six lanterns shine at once, and the whole round table glows. A beam of light rises from the center of the table, up through the clouds, to one bright star high above. Orbit whispers, That star shows where every journey began. Now, phonics. Let's review. Renewable is re plus new plus able. One billion has nine zeros. Let me give an example: stress AM in exAMple. Finally starts the last point, so pause after the comma. Possibly means maybe, but less sure. Goodbye, Hall of the Round Table! I wonder what that star could be.
